panels.title: Big questions
points: Who decides which history we learn?
How can a story outlive the person who tells it?
How can something as ordinary as water feel like a miracle?
Should clean water be a right for everyone?

panels.title: Islamic foundation
panels.text: The Qur'an tells many stories of past peoples and says: 'There was certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding' (Yusuf 12:111). Knowing history, including the history of Muslim civilisation, helps us understand who we are.

panels.title: Checking Out Me History: identity and heritage
points: John Agard, born in 1949 in Guyana, then British Guiana
Moved to Britain in 1977
Often uses Caribbean dialect and spelling
Short, repetitive stanzas for the taught history

panels.title: If I Must Die: hope, memory and legacy
points: Refaat Alareer (1979 to 2023), born in Gaza
Taught English literature and creative writing
Mentored young writers to tell their stories
Killed in an airstrike in Gaza, December 2023

panels.title: Blessing: water, scarcity and gratitude
points: Imtiaz Dharker: born in Lahore, grew up in Glasgow
Has lived and worked in Mumbai
A water pipe bursts in a poor district
Everyone rushes out to collect the water

panels.title: Non-fiction: clean water and human rights
points: In 2010 the UN recognised water and sanitation as human rights
In 2022, 2.2 billion people lacked safely managed drinking water
Women and girls often walk to fetch water
Clean water reduces disease and keeps children in school

panels.title: How does Agard present identity?
points: Point: Agard presents identity as something taken back
Evidence: 'I carving out me identity'
Technique: metaphor; first-person dialect
Zoom in: 'carving' suggests hard, lasting work, like stone

Answer: Agard presents identity as something the speaker must take back: the metaphor 'I carving out me identity' suggests effort and permanence, as if the speaker sculpts a self that the taught history had hidden.

panels.title: How does Alareer structure the poem to present legacy?
points: Point: the poem moves from death towards hope
Evidence: opens 'If I must die' and ends 'let it be a tale'
Structural strategy: conditional opening; hopeful ending
Analyse: the poem refuses to end in death

Answer: Alareer structures the poem so that it travels from death to hope: the conditional 'If I must die' opens it, but the final plea 'let it be a tale' closes it, so the poem itself becomes the story that outlives him.

panels.title: How does Dharker present water as precious?
points: Point: Dharker presents water as a rare gift
Evidence: 'There never is enough water.'
Technique: short declarative sentence
Zoom in: 'never' makes scarcity constant

Answer: Dharker presents water as a rare gift: the short declarative 'There never is enough water' makes scarcity a constant fact, so when the pipe bursts the people's joy feels like receiving a blessing.

panels.title: Compare how two poets present the importance of stories.
points: Theme: both explore stories that might be lost
Attitude: Agard angry then proud; Alareer calm and hopeful
Poetic methods: dialect and repetition / symbol and plea
Structure: drilled lists to a breakaway voice / a condition to a hope

Answer: Both Agard and Alareer present stories as precious and fragile. Agard, at first angry and finally proud, uses dialect and repetition to reclaim a hidden history, whereas Alareer calmly uses the symbol of a kite and a plea to ask that his own story survive.
